lead: Every power switch loses energy twice: once while it turns on and once while it turns off. During those short transitions, voltage across the device and current through it are both nonzero, so they multiply into heat. Switching loss is that heat per second. Thermal design carries it from the tiny junction to the air without letting the junction exceed its limit. This matters in switch-mode power supplies, motor drives, inverters and chargers, including the charger brick for a phone or an electric scooter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for device conduction models and Chapter 1.7 for snubber energy and ratings.

blocks.text: An ideal switch drops zero volts when on and carries zero current when off. A real switch spends a short time between these states. During turn-on, current rises while voltage is still high. During turn-off, voltage rises while current still flows. The product v × i is power, so each transition gives a pulse of heat.

Use the triangular approximation for one transition: E = 0.5 × V × I × t. E is energy in joules, V is blocking voltage in volts, I is load current in amperes, and t is transition time in seconds. Turn-on energy is E_on = 0.5 × V × I × t_on. Turn-off energy is E_off = 0.5 × V × I × t_off.
E_on = 0.5 × V × I × t_on,   E_off = 0.5 × V × I × t_off
blocks.where: E_on and E_off are transition energies in J; V is blocking voltage in V; I is load current in A; t_on and t_off are transition times in s.

blocks.text: Average switching power multiplies the energy of all transitions in one cycle by the number of cycles per second.
P_sw = (E_on + E_off) × f_s = 0.5 × V × I × (t_on + t_off) × f_s
blocks.where: P_sw is average switching power in W; f_s is switching frequency in Hz; E_on and E_off are transition energies in J.

blocks.text: Use the total transition time inside the bracket. Do not use t_on alone when t_off is nonzero. A 10 kHz switch has 10,000 turn-on events and 10,000 turn-off events each second. Shorter edges (smaller t_on, t_off) reduce P_sw, but faster edges increase dv/dt and di/dt; snubbers and layout then matter, as in Chapter 1.7. Switching loss rises linearly with f_s. At high frequency it can exceed conduction loss.

sections.h3: Add conduction loss to get total heat

blocks.text: While the device is fully on, it still has a voltage drop. For a diode, thyristor, BJT or IGBT, P_cond = V_on × I × D. V_on is the on-state drop in volts, I is the average current while the device conducts (the on-interval) in amperes, and D is duty ratio, the fraction of the period the device conducts. If the current you have is already the average over the whole period, do not multiply by D again.

For a MOSFET, use its channel resistance: P_cond = I_rms² × R_on × D. I_rms is the rms current during the on-interval in amperes and R_on is on-resistance in ohms. If the rms you have is taken over the whole period, D must not be multiplied in again. In a switch-mode converter, D is set by the conversion ratio; see Unit 3, DC-DC converters.

blocks.where: P_total is total device loss in W; P_cond is conduction loss in W; P_sw is switching loss in W.

blocks.text: P_total is the heat that the thermal path must remove. Gate-drive loss is small and is not repeated here. For a first design, use the worst-case load current and the highest ambient temperature expected. Use the same units before adding: watts with watts, amperes with amperes.

Heat is generated at the semiconductor junction. It travels through the device case, through the mounting interface, into the heat sink, and then to the surrounding air. Each step has a thermal resistance Rθ, measured in °C/W. A thermal resistance of 1 °C/W means 1 W of heat raises that layer's temperature by 1 °C above the next layer.

The three series resistances are Rθ_JC from junction to case, Rθ_CS from case to heat sink, and Rθ_SA from heat sink to ambient. Some texts write Rθ_sa or R_th(h-a) for the same heat-sink-to-ambient resistance. Thermal resistances add like series resistors. The steady-state junction temperature follows from that sum.

blocks.where: T_j is junction temperature in °C; T_a is ambient temperature in °C; P_total is total loss in W; Rθ_JC, Rθ_CS and Rθ_SA are thermal resistances in °C/W.

blocks.text: To choose a heat sink, rearrange the formula: Rθ_SA ≤ (T_j,max − T_a)/P_total − Rθ_JC − Rθ_CS. T_j,max is the datasheet limit, often 125 °C or 150 °C. A lower Rθ_SA means a larger heat sink, more fins, or more airflow. The case-to-heat-sink value depends on the thermal pad and mounting pressure.

For a short pulse, the junction does not heat instantly. Datasheets give transient thermal impedance Zθ_JC(t), which is lower than Rθ_JC for times shorter than the thermal time constant. Use Zθ_JC for single pulses and for repeated pulses with low duty ratio. For steady-state design, use the sum of the Rθ values.

figure.caption: Heat flows from the junction through the case and heat sink to ambient; each layer adds thermal resistance. The values match the worked example, so the heat-sink resistance is the one to choose.

spec.aria: Heat flows from the device junction through the case and heat sink to ambient; each layer adds thermal resistance.

examples.question: A MOSFET switches V = 200 V and I = 10 A. Turn-on time is 1 μs and turn-off time is 2 μs. Switching frequency is 10 kHz. Ambient is 40 °C, junction-to-case Rθ_JC = 1.0 °C/W, case-to-heat-sink Rθ_CS = 0.5 °C/W. The junction limit is 125 °C. Find the switching power loss and the maximum heat-sink thermal resistance Rθ_SA allowed. Ignore conduction loss for this calculation.
steps: Total transition time: t_on + t_off = 1 μs + 2 μs = 3 μs = 3 × 10⁻⁶ s.
Switching energy per cycle: E_cycle = 0.5 × 200 V × 10 A × 3 × 10⁻⁶ s = 0.003 J.
Switching power: P_sw = E_cycle × f_s = 0.003 J × 10,000 Hz = 30 W.
Allowed total thermal resistance: Rθ_total = (T_j,max − T_a)/P_sw = (125 − 40)/30 = 85/30 = 2.833 °C/W.
Rθ_SA ≤ 2.833 − 1.5 = 1.33 °C/W. Choose a heat sink rated at or below 1.33 °C/W.
examples.answer: P_sw = 30 W and the heat sink must have Rθ_SA ≤ 1.33 °C/W.
examples.check:
V = 200.0
I = 10.0
t_on = 1e-6
t_off = 2e-6
f_s = 10e3
T_a = 40.0
T_jmax = 125.0
Rθ_JC = 1.0
Rθ_CS = 0.5
P_sw = 0.5 * V * I * (t_on + t_off) * f_s
Rθ_total = (T_jmax - T_a) / P_sw
Rθ_SA = Rθ_total - Rθ_JC - Rθ_CS
print(P_sw)
print(round(Rθ_total, 3))
print(round(Rθ_SA, 2))

traps: Adding only t_on and forgetting t_off. Add t_on + t_off in the total transition time. Leaving out t_off always underestimates P_sw, and it halves the answer when t_on = t_off.
Putting f_s in kHz. 10 kHz is 10,000 Hz; a factor of 1000 error changes P_sw by 1000.
Adding thermal resistances in parallel. Rθ_JC, Rθ_CS and Rθ_SA are in series, so they add.
Thinking a lower Rθ_SA means a smaller heat sink. Lower resistance needs more metal surface, more fins, or more airflow.
Using Rθ_JC for a short pulse. Use Zθ_JC(t) from the transient curve for pulse widths well below the thermal time constant.

quiz.q: State the triangular formula for the energy lost in one switching transition and define each symbol.
quiz.a: E = 0.5 × V × I × t. E is energy in J, V is blocking voltage in V, I is current in A, and t is transition time in s.

quiz.q: Why does switching loss rise when f_s rises if t_on and t_off stay the same?
quiz.a: Each cycle still has the same energy per transition, but there are more cycles per second. Power is energy per second, so P_sw rises in direct proportion to f_s.

quiz.q: A switch has V = 100 V, I = 5 A, t_on = 2 μs, t_off = 1 μs, f_s = 20 kHz. Find P_sw with the triangular approximation.
In the worked example, keep P = 30 W and Rθ_JC = 1.0 °C/W, but change Rθ_CS to 0.3 °C/W. Find the maximum Rθ_SA for T_j ≤ 125 °C and T_a = 40 °C.
A designer doubles f_s while keeping V, I, t_on and t_off fixed. Conduction loss is unchanged. What happens to P_total and to the required Rθ_SA?
quiz.a: P_sw doubles, so P_total rises. For a fixed T_j,max and T_a, the allowed total thermal resistance falls, so Rθ_SA must be smaller: a bigger heat sink or more airflow is needed.

quiz.q: Why can a device survive a short overload pulse that would be too much in steady state?
quiz.a: The junction has thermal mass. For short times the transient thermal impedance Zθ_JC(t) is lower than the steady-state Rθ_JC, so the temperature rise is smaller.

quiz.q: Name the three thermal resistances from junction to ambient and give their symbols.
quiz.a: Junction-to-case Rθ_JC, case-to-heat-sink Rθ_CS, and heat-sink-to-ambient Rθ_SA.

quiz.q: A datasheet gives Rθ_JC = 1.5 °C/W, Rθ_CS = 0.4 °C/W, and a heat sink of 2.0 °C/W. Ambient is 45 °C and P = 20 W. Is T_j below 120 °C?

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, thermal design uses datasheet transient curves and finite-element simulation of heat sinks, not just one steady-state number. Wide band-gap devices such as SiC and GaN switch faster, so switching loss falls but layout and thermal density become harder. Search next for transient thermal impedance, thermal via PCB, and junction temperature calculation. Electric-vehicle traction inverters and server power supplies are common places where this chapter's arithmetic decides the heat-sink size.
